verses.text: David said, “Is there yet any who is left of Saul’s house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
There was of Saul’s house a servant whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David; and the king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” He said, “I am your servant.”
The king said, “Is there not yet any of Saul’s house, that I may show the kindness of God to him?” Ziba said to the king, “Jonathan still has a son, who is lame in his feet.”
The king said to him, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “Behold, he is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, in Lo Debar.”
Then king David sent, and brought him out of the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo Debar.
Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, and fell on his face, and showed respect. David said, “Mephibosheth.” He answered, “Behold, your servant!”

David said to him, “Don’t be afraid of him; for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake, and will restore to you all the land of Saul your father. You will eat bread at my table continually.”
He bowed down, and said, “What is your servant, that you should look at such a dead dog as I am?”
Then the king called to Ziba, Saul’s servant, and said to him, “All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master’s son.

Till the land for him, you, your sons, and your servants. Bring in the harvest, that your master’s son may have bread to eat; but Mephibosheth your master’s son will always eat bread at my table.” Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Then Ziba said to the king, “According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so your servant will do.” So Mephibosheth ate at the king’s table, like one of the king’s sons.
Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Mica. All that lived in Ziba’s house were servants to Mephibosheth.
So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem; for he ate continually at the king’s table. He was lame in both his feet.

footnotes.content: David's first thought after securing his throne is not to consolidate power, but to keep an old promise. Kindness for Jonathan's sake—the covenant between them runs deeper than victory and thrones. It shows us where a true leader's heart rests when the fighting is done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ziba appears from Saul's household—not an enemy, but a servant caught in the tangle of old loyalties. David calls on him directly: Are you Ziba? The king himself speaks to a servant with respect, seeking someone who might know the hidden branches of Saul's family.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The 'kindness of God'—not just political favor, but something deeper, more eternal. Ziba mentions Jonathan's son is lame, as if it were a barrier. But to David, it's no barrier at all; the disability changes nothing about his debt to Jonathan or his word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mephibosheth hides in Lo Debar—a name meaning 'no pasture,' a place of scarcity and forgetting. The son of a king lives in exile, concealed. He was a boy when his father died at Gilboa; all his life, he's carried the shame of defeat and the fear of a rival's sword.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David sends for him—personally, with the full authority of the crown. What must have raced through Mephibosheth's mind? Does he expect judgment? Exile? Worse? Yet the king commands his retrieval with the weight of his throne behind it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mephibosheth falls on his face in reverence and terror. David uses his name—a small kindness, but it means the king knows him, has thought of him. In that moment, the shame of exile begins to lift, though Mephibosheth cannot yet see it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David speaks the word that changes everything: 'Don't be afraid.' Lands restored, a table at the king's own house, daily bread—all because of a dead man's covenant with a living one. This is grace written in real property and real meals, not merely words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'A dead dog'—Mephibosheth sees himself through the lens of his lameness and exile, worthless in the eyes of the world. Yet David has already looked past all that. The man calls himself what he believes; the king names what is true: beloved, restored, a place at the table.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All that belonged to Saul—flocks, fields, households, a father's whole estate—now flows to Jonathan's son through David's hand. Ziba, the servant, will work the land so that Mephibosheth may eat. The old king's ruin becomes the pathway to the young prince's provision.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David speaks to Ziba, but his words are for Mephibosheth's ears: the land will be tilled, harvests brought in, and still he will eat at the royal table. More than provision—belonging. A place in the king's presence, daily, without end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mephibosheth ate at the king's table like one of the king's sons—not as a servant, not as a favor, but as family. The exile has ended. After years in Lo Debar, he has come home to a place he never expected to know.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mephibosheth has a son, Mica. The line continues. What was meant to end in shame—a crippled man with no future, no place—now opens into a family, a legacy. Ziba's household serves Mephibosheth, and through him, serves the promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this: a man crippled, forgotten, brought from nothing into the king's daily fellowship—fed at his table, never cast out. We know a kinship like that, too, written in bread and wine, rest and belonging that runs deeper than what we deserve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
